blocks.content: The load-balancer-networking topic briefly mentioned that load balancers are often implemented specifically as a reverse proxy. This topic covers the reverse proxy concept properly in its own right, a server that sits in front of one or more backend servers, handling incoming requests on their behalf.
A reverse proxy is one of the most common, foundational pieces of real production infrastructure, quietly sitting between the outside world and an application actual backend servers.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437997518-428060320.png
1. What a Reverse Proxy Actually Does
blocks.text: 1. What a Reverse Proxy Actually Does

blocks.content: A reverse proxy sits directly in front of one or more backend servers, receiving incoming client requests on their behalf and forwarding them to the appropriate actual server behind it. The client only ever interacts with the reverse proxy itself, never directly with the real backend servers doing the actual work.
2. Hiding the Real Backend Servers

The real backend servers, their actual number, their actual addresses, their actual internal configuration, are hidden entirely from the outside world. The client only ever sees and interacts with the reverse proxy sitting in front, with no visibility into what is actually happening behind it.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437997521-662208386.png
3. The Direct Connection to Load Balancing
blocks.text: 3. The Direct Connection to Load Balancing

blocks.content: A load balancer, covered in the previous topic, is very often implemented specifically as a reverse proxy. It sits in exactly this same front facing position, both distributing traffic across multiple backend servers AND hiding those real servers from direct outside exposure at the same time, two closely related jobs performed by the same piece of infrastructure.

4. TLS Termination: Handling Encryption at the Proxy
blocks.text: 4. TLS Termination: Handling Encryption at the Proxy

blocks.content: A genuinely common, practical role for a reverse proxy is TLS termination. Encrypted HTTPS traffic, covered in full in the ssl-tls-handshake topic, arrives at the reverse proxy, which handles the actual handshake and decryption itself, then talks to the backend servers behind it over plain, unencrypted traffic internally, since that internal traffic never actually leaves the genuinely trusted internal network.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437997524-903869205.png
blocks.alt: TLS Termination: Handling Encryption at the Proxy

blocks.title: Why this is genuinely practical, not a security shortcut
blocks.content: Handling encryption and decryption in one central place, rather than on every single backend server individually, is simpler to manage and update, and the internal traffic between the proxy and backend servers stays within a genuinely trusted, private network boundary.
5. Caching at the Proxy Layer

A reverse proxy can also cache repeated responses directly itself. If many different clients request the exact same piece of content, the reverse proxy can serve it directly from its own cache, without needing to forward every single one of those repeated requests all the way back to a backend server.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437997525-629617033.png

blocks.title: The same caching principle as caching topics earlier in this course
blocks.content: This is a direct, real world application of the same caching principle covered elsewhere, avoid repeating expensive work, applied specifically at the network boundary between clients and backend servers.
6. A Genuine Security Benefit

Backend servers exposed directly to the internet present a real, larger attack surface, every single one of them individually reachable and probeable. A reverse proxy sitting in front instead means the real backend servers are genuinely shielded from direct exposure, with only the proxy itself actually facing the outside world.

7. A Real World Analogy

A visitor to a large office building talks only to the front desk receptionist, who then routes them internally to the correct specific person or department. The visitor never wanders the building looking for the right office directly, exactly like a client only ever talking to the reverse proxy, which handles routing to the correct backend server internally.

Assuming a reverse proxy only ever does load balancing, when TLS termination, caching, and hiding backend servers are all genuinely common, separate roles it can play.
A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers, receiving requests on their behalf and hiding them from direct outside exposure.
It is often combined with load balancing, TLS termination, and caching, all in one piece of infrastructure.
Backend servers behind a reverse proxy have a genuinely smaller, better protected attack surface.
